summary: Defines a general way to locate an application service by domain name, without relying on rigid naming conventions known as name hacks. It uses SRV records and the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System to map a domain, service name, and protocol to a target server and port.

eli5.summary: Instead of guessing that the mail server is called mail.example, you ask the phone book which computer handles mail for that company and which door to knock on.

questions: how to find a service by domain name
how do naptr and srv records work together

how does a client find a server using ddds
subtitle: How a client turns a domain, a service name and a protocol into a server and port, using NAPTR and SRV records.

tldr.problem: Clients need to find the server for an application service in a domain without relying on rigid naming conventions (name hacks), and SRV records alone allow only one layer of indirection.
tldr.mechanism: S-NAPTR is a Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) application. The client looks up NAPTR records for the domain, matches a service and protocol tag, follows replacements until a terminal S or A flag, then resolves SRV or address records to get host and port.
tldr.outcome: Domain operators can rank protocols and hand parts of a service to another organization, and clients backtrack to the next target on failure. The RFC has been updated by RFC 8553.

facts.label: Registries
facts.value: Application service tags and application protocol tags

today: RFC 3958 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8553. The RFC itself describes its two IANA registries for application service and protocol tags.

sections.title: Why Name Hacks Are Not Enough
sections.content:
RFC 3958 defines a general way to name application services so that a client can find them without relying on rigid domain naming conventions, which the RFC calls name hacks. It does this with a Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) Application that maps a domain name, an application service name and an application protocol to a target server and port.

The application combines two kinds of DNS resource records: NAPTR records and SRV records. The RFC describes it as a more general version of the use of SRV, and also as a very restricted use of NAPTR. The restricted form is called S-NAPTR, for Straightforward NAPTR.
sections.eli5: It is a standard way to ask the internet's phone book where a service lives, so nobody has to guess computer names.

sections.title: Application Services and Protocols
sections.content:
An application service is a generic type of application, independent of the protocol that offers it. Each service is tied to an IANA-registered tag. Retrieving mail is the RFC's example: it can be done with POP3 or IMAP4, and a tag such as RetMail could be registered for it. The RFC notes that this has not been done and that there are no plans to do so.

An application protocol implements the service and also gets a registered tag. If several transports are available, separate tags should be defined for each. The pair of tags, such as RetMail:POP3, should be specific enough for a client to identify a server it can talk to.

Some protocols support several services. LDAP is the RFC's example, found supporting services such as white pages.
sections.eli5: A service is what you want to do, like reading mail. A protocol is the language you use to do it. You need both to find the right helper.

sections.title: Resolving with NAPTR and SRV
sections.content:
The client retrieves all NAPTR records for the target domain and sorts them by increasing ORDER, and by increasing PREF within each ORDER. Starting from the first record, it checks the SERVICE field for the desired application service and a protocol it supports. Matching records are processed in sort order.

The FLAG field decides what happens next. An empty flag makes the record non-terminal: the REPLACEMENT field is the target of the next NAPTR lookup. In S-NAPTR the only terminal flags are S and A. With S, the replacement is looked up for SRV records and normal SRV processing applies. With A, an address record is sought for the replacement and the default protocol port is assumed.

Targets are pursued in order until a server is contacted or all matching records are exhausted, so a client must backtrack on failure. Failure is declared when the server cannot provide security credentials for the originating domain, when the connection otherwise fails, or when a DNS lookup returns nothing expected. A client that supports several protocols MUST finish resolution for one protocol before trying another, and the protocol it picks MUST be listed in the first NAPTR set.
sections.eli5: You follow a trail of signposts, best one first. Some signposts point to more signposts and some point to the actual door. If a door is locked or fake, you go back and try the next trail.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three use cases: finding the authoritative server for a service within a domain, offering a service over multiple protocols, and remote hosting by another organization. Its hypothetical extensible messaging service (tag EM) shows the last two. The domain thinkingcat.example runs its own ProtA servers but relies on example.com for ProtB and ProtC.

With NAPTR in front of SRV, thinkingcat.example states its preference ranking across protocols while the outsourcer ranks its own servers independently in SRV records. The RFC says this independence cannot be achieved with SRV records alone.

A better remote-hosting layout has a single NAPTR record in thinkingcat.example, with service EM:ProtB:ProtC, pointing at the hosting domain. The hosting domain then keeps NAPTR records for each protocol and can change its hosts from time to time. The RFC also shows a domain publishing several services in one NAPTR set, where the client sorts by ORDER and uses the first matching record with the lowest PREF.
sections.eli5: A company can say "for chat, ask my friend's company". The friend's company decides which of its own computers answers, and can change that whenever it likes.

sections.title: Why Not Just SRV or Just NAPTR
sections.content:
SRV records let a domain move services between hosts, run several servers and mark backups. The RFC lists their limits for this purpose. SRV gives a single layer of indirection, aims at server administration rather than application naming, and ties service and protocol to terms that imply UDP or TCP, which is insufficient for these use cases.

NAPTR records cannot appear in the wild on their own; they must be part of a DDDS application. They also carry powerful rewrite rules, and that power (the RFC writes it as complexity) makes designers and administrators nervous because of noodle-like rule sets that are hard to test. S-NAPTR therefore allows only replacement expressions, not regular expressions. This keeps client resolution predictable and efficient.
sections.eli5: SRV is a short signpost with only one step. NAPTR can do clever tricks but is easy to get tangled. S-NAPTR uses the simple parts of NAPTR so it stays easy to follow.

sections.title: The Formal DDDS Definition
sections.content:
The Application-Unique String is the domain label for which a server is sought, and the First Well-Known Rule is identity, so the output is that same domain. The expected output is what a client needs to connect: host, port and protocol. Only the S and A flags are valid, and only substitution rules are permitted. The one database is NAPTR records in DNS, keyed by domain names.

The Service Parameters string is an optional app-service followed by zero or more app-protocol tags, separated by :. Tags are limited to 32 characters, must start with a letter and are case-insensitive. Tags starting with x- are experimental. The colon is the separator because +, used in the URI DDDS application of RFC 3404, is allowed in URI scheme names.

DNS servers MAY use the flag values to add the relevant NAPTR, SRV or A records to the Additional Information section of a response. Clients are encouraged, not required, to check for it.
sections.eli5: The rules are short: start with the company's domain, use only two kinds of end signs, and write the service label in a fixed simple pattern.

sections.title: IANA Registries and Guidelines
sections.content:
The RFC calls for two IANA registries: one for application service tags and one for application protocol tags. Each lists the tag and the defining publication, which is the RFC that defined it. Tags beginning with x- are experimental and nothing prevents duplicate use, so implementors use them at their own risk.

All other tags use the specification required policy from RFC 2434, where the specification must be an RFC of any category. That RFC must describe each tag, its intended usage, interoperability and security considerations, and related publications.

The guidelines add that protocol developers must document when a client retries or fails over, and the handshake that identifies the server. Domain administrators are told to keep NAPTR and SRV trees small: fewer branches, and shallower trees, using NAPTR to identify services hosted elsewhere rather than to rename services within a zone.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of service and protocol names so everyone spells them the same way. Names starting with x- are scratch names anyone can use, at their own risk.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The approach is only as secure as the DNS queries along the way. If any is compromised, bogus NAPTR and SRV records could redirect clients to unintended destinations. DNSSEC can be used to ensure that the records are valid.

With or without DNSSEC, applications should define end-to-end authentication. The basic mechanism has the client send the original name of the desired destination during the handshake, with no transformations from NAPTR replacements, SRV targets or CNAME changes. Where the protocol has no such feature but TLS may be used, the server_name TLS extension can carry it. The server returns a credential with the appropriate name, such as an X.509 certificate or a Kerberos service principal name. The client compares names using the protocol's matching rules, and if they match and the credentials have integrity there is reasonable assurance that the right endpoint was reached.

This RFC does not define the handshake, the credential fields or the matching rules. Definitions of S-NAPTR for particular protocols MUST define them.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can fake the phone book could send you to the wrong door. So when you get there, you ask the person at the door to prove they really work for the company you asked about.
